📄 2. Introduction

Anemia is one of the most common nutritional and hematological disorders worldwide. It is a condition in which the blood does not have enough healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin to carry adequate oxygen to body tissues. Hemoglobin is an iron-containing protein present in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to different parts of the body. When hemoglobin level decreases, the tissues receive less oxygen, which results in weakness, fatigue, dizziness, breathlessness and reduced work capacity.

Anemia may affect people of all age groups, but it is more common among infants, children, adolescent girls, pregnant women, lactating mothers and women of reproductive age. In India, anemia is a major public health problem due to poor nutrition, iron deficiency, worm infestation, repeated pregnancies, heavy menstrual bleeding and lack of awareness about iron-rich foods. Nurses play an important role in early identification, prevention, treatment support and health education regarding anemia.

📄 3. Definition

Anemia is defined as a condition in which the hemoglobin concentration, red blood cell count or packed cell volume is below normal for age and sex, resulting in decreased oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

📄 4. Normal Hemoglobin Values

Group Normal Hemoglobin Level
Adult Male13–17 g/dL
Adult Female12–15 g/dL
Pregnant Woman11 g/dL or above
Children11–13 g/dL
Newborn14–20 g/dL

📄 5. Epidemiology / Incidence

Anemia is widely prevalent in developing countries and is commonly associated with nutritional deficiency. Iron deficiency anemia is the most common type of anemia. It is frequently seen in adolescent girls due to menstrual blood loss and poor dietary intake. Pregnant women are also at high risk because of increased iron requirement during pregnancy. Children may develop anemia due to poor nutrition, worm infestation, recurrent infections and rapid growth.

📄 6. Pathophysiology

In anemia, the number of red blood cells or hemoglobin level decreases. As a result, the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood is reduced. The body tissues receive less oxygen, leading to tissue hypoxia. To compensate for low oxygen supply, the heart increases its rate and force of contraction. This may cause palpitation, tachycardia and breathlessness. If anemia becomes severe and remains untreated, it may lead to cardiac stress, poor growth, reduced immunity and complications during pregnancy.

📄 7. Causes of Anemia

  • Iron deficiency: Inadequate intake of iron-rich foods is the most common cause.
  • Blood loss: Heavy menstruation, injury, surgery, piles or gastrointestinal bleeding may cause anemia.
  • Pregnancy: Increased demand for iron and folic acid during pregnancy may cause anemia.
  • Vitamin deficiency: Deficiency of vitamin B12 and folic acid causes megaloblastic anemia.
  • Worm infestation: Hookworm infestation causes chronic blood loss.
  • Chronic diseases: Kidney disease, tuberculosis, cancer and chronic inflammatory diseases may cause anemia.
  • Hemolysis: Excessive destruction of red blood cells may cause hemolytic anemia.
  • Bone marrow failure: Aplastic anemia occurs when bone marrow fails to produce enough blood cells.
  • Inherited disorders: Thalassemia and sickle cell disease may cause chronic anemia.

📄 8. Risk Factors

  • Poor dietary intake
  • Low socio-economic status
  • Adolescent age group
  • Pregnancy and lactation
  • Repeated pregnancies with short birth spacing
  • Heavy menstrual bleeding
  • Worm infestation
  • Chronic infection
  • Lack of awareness about balanced diet
  • Vegetarian diet without proper iron sources

📄 9. Classification / Types of Anemia

A. According to Cause

  • Nutritional anemia: Due to deficiency of iron, folic acid or vitamin B12.
  • Hemorrhagic anemia: Due to acute or chronic blood loss.
  • Hemolytic anemia: Due to increased destruction of red blood cells.
  • Aplastic anemia: Due to bone marrow failure.
  • Anemia of chronic disease: Due to chronic infection, kidney disease or inflammatory disease.

B. According to Red Blood Cell Size

  • Microcytic anemia: Red blood cells are smaller than normal, commonly seen in iron deficiency anemia.
  • Normocytic anemia: Red blood cells are normal in size but reduced in number.
  • Macrocytic anemia: Red blood cells are larger than normal, commonly seen in vitamin B12 or folic acid deficiency.

📄 10. Signs and Symptoms

  • General weakness and fatigue
  • Pallor of skin, conjunctiva, tongue and nail beds
  • Dizziness or fainting tendency
  • Shortness of breath on exertion
  • Palpitation
  • Headache
  • Cold hands and feet
  • Loss of appetite
  • Irritability
  • Poor concentration
  • Brittle nails
  • Hair fall
  • Pica, such as craving for mud, chalk or ice
  • Delayed growth and development in children

📄 11. Diagnostic Evaluation

  • Complete Blood Count: Helps to assess hemoglobin, RBC count, hematocrit and red cell indices.
  • Hemoglobin Estimation: Confirms severity of anemia.
  • Peripheral Blood Smear: Shows size, shape and appearance of red blood cells.
  • Serum Ferritin: Indicates iron stores in the body.
  • Serum Iron and TIBC: Helps in diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia.
  • Vitamin B12 and Folate Level: Done when megaloblastic anemia is suspected.
  • Stool Examination: Done to detect occult blood and worm infestation.
  • Reticulocyte Count: Shows bone marrow response.
  • Bone Marrow Examination: Done in selected cases such as aplastic anemia.

📄 12. Severity of Anemia

Severity Hemoglobin Level
Mild Anemia10–10.9 g/dL
Moderate Anemia7–9.9 g/dL
Severe AnemiaLess than 7 g/dL

📄 13. Medical Management / Treatment

  • Identify and treat the underlying cause of anemia.
  • Give oral iron and folic acid tablets as prescribed.
  • Give vitamin B12 injection or supplements if deficiency is present.
  • Provide deworming medicine if worm infestation is suspected or confirmed.
  • Treat chronic infections and inflammatory conditions.
  • Advise iron-rich and protein-rich diet.
  • Blood transfusion may be required in severe anemia or emergency conditions.
  • Monitor hemoglobin level regularly.
  • Refer complicated or severe cases to higher health facility.

📄 14. Nursing Management

  • Assess general condition of the patient.
  • Observe for pallor, weakness, dizziness and breathlessness.
  • Monitor vital signs regularly.
  • Assess dietary pattern and nutritional status.
  • Encourage adequate rest and sleep.
  • Plan activities according to patient tolerance.
  • Administer iron, folic acid or vitamin B12 as prescribed.
  • Observe side effects of iron therapy such as nausea, constipation and black stool.
  • Encourage intake of iron-rich foods and vitamin C rich foods.
  • Advise patient to avoid tea or coffee immediately after meals.
  • Maintain hygiene and prevent infection.
  • Educate patient and family regarding prevention of anemia.
  • Encourage regular follow-up and hemoglobin testing.

Explain importance of IFA tablets, diet, deworming and follow-up. Knowledge improves compliance and prevents recurrence. Patient explained preventive measures correctly.

📄 16. Diet Plan for Anemia

Diet plays an important role in prevention and treatment of anemia. The patient should take iron-rich foods along with vitamin C rich foods because vitamin C increases iron absorption. Protein-rich foods are also important for blood formation and general health.

Food Group Examples
Iron-rich foodsGreen leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates, raisins, sesame seeds, groundnuts
Protein-rich foodsDal, pulses, beans, milk, curd, egg, fish, meat
Vitamin C rich foodsLemon, amla, orange, guava, tomato
Folic acid sourcesGreen leafy vegetables, legumes, citrus fruits
Vitamin B12 sourcesMilk, curd, egg, meat, fish

📄 17. Prevention of Anemia

  • Take balanced diet rich in iron, protein and vitamins.
  • Take iron and folic acid tablets regularly as advised.
  • Consume vitamin C rich foods with meals.
  • Avoid tea and coffee immediately after meals because they reduce iron absorption.
  • Maintain personal hygiene and environmental sanitation.
  • Use footwear to prevent hookworm infestation.
  • Take deworming medicine as advised by health worker.
  • Attend antenatal check-ups during pregnancy.
  • Maintain proper spacing between pregnancies.
  • Screen adolescent girls, pregnant women and children for anemia.
  • Treat heavy menstrual bleeding and chronic infections early.

📄 18. Health Education

  • Explain the meaning, causes and symptoms of anemia.
  • Teach the importance of iron-rich diet.
  • Advise regular intake of prescribed iron and folic acid tablets.
  • Explain that iron tablets may cause black stool, which is usually normal.
  • Advise taking iron tablets after meals if gastric irritation occurs.
  • Encourage intake of lemon water, amla or guava with meals to increase iron absorption.
  • Advise not to take tea or coffee immediately after meals.
  • Encourage deworming and use of footwear.
  • Teach menstrual hygiene and advise medical consultation for heavy bleeding.
  • Encourage pregnant women to attend regular antenatal visits.
  • Advise follow-up hemoglobin testing.

📄 19. Complications of Anemia

  • Severe weakness and fatigue
  • Reduced work capacity
  • Increased risk of infection
  • Heart failure in severe anemia
  • Poor pregnancy outcome
  • Preterm birth
  • Low birth weight baby
  • Postpartum complications
  • Delayed growth and development in children
  • Poor school performance and reduced concentration

📄 20. Role of Nurse in Prevention and Control of Anemia

  • Screen high-risk groups for anemia.
  • Identify signs and symptoms of anemia early.
  • Provide iron and folic acid tablets as per health programme.
  • Educate adolescent girls, pregnant women and mothers about anemia prevention.
  • Promote balanced diet and locally available iron-rich foods.
  • Encourage deworming and sanitation practices.
  • Monitor compliance with iron therapy.
  • Refer severe anemia cases to higher health facility.
  • Maintain records and follow-up of anemic patients.
  • Conduct health education sessions in school and community.

📄 21. Conclusion

Anemia is a common but preventable and treatable health problem. It mainly occurs due to iron deficiency, poor nutrition, blood loss, worm infestation and increased demand during pregnancy. Early diagnosis, proper treatment, iron and folic acid supplementation, balanced diet, deworming and health education are essential for prevention and control of anemia. Nurses have an important role in assessment, treatment support, counselling, follow-up and community awareness regarding anemia.
